questions.q: Why write automated tests instead of running the code and reading the output?
questions.explain: Every change can break something that used to work, and nobody re-checks forty endpoints by hand after each commit. Tests do it before every commit and on every pull request.
options: Automated tests make the code run faster in production
You write them once, and they re-check everything in seconds after every change
Tests replace the need for code review
Node.js refuses to run code without tests

questions.q: A test checks that the task store's SQL returns only the current user's tasks from a PGlite database. What kind of test is it?
questions.explain: Your code working together with a real database is an integration test. It is slower than a unit test but catches SQL typos and broken constraints.

questions.q: A test sends GET /v1/tasks?limit=0 over HTTP and checks for a 400 problem details body. What kind of test is it?
questions.explain: It tests the whole system from the outside, the way a client uses it. End-to-end tests are the slowest, so projects write only a few of them.

questions.q: What mix of tests does the lesson recommend for most projects?
questions.explain: Fast unit tests catch most bugs; the slower integration and end-to-end tests prove that the parts really fit together.
options: Only end-to-end tests, because they test everything
Many unit tests, a good number of integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests
Only unit tests, because they are fast
The same number of each kind

questions.q: This is the lesson's assertEqual. What does it print?
questions.explain: The first check passes, because trim removes the trailing space. In the second, the two spaces in the middle become two dashes. Here the test found a real bug in slug.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: === compares objects by identity: two separate objects are never equal, even with the same content. That is why assert has deepEqual, which compares content.

questions.q: Why does the lesson import node:assert/strict rather than plain node:assert?
questions.explain: Loose comparison would let a string "1" pass where the number 1 was expected, hiding real bugs.
options: It compares with ===, so 1 and "1" are not treated as equal
The plain version does not have deepEqual
The strict version works in the browser only

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: assert.equal in strict mode is ===: a number is not a string, and two different arrays are different objects. A failed assertion throws an AssertionError with the code ERR_ASSERTION.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: deepEqual compares objects and arrays by content, all the way down. In strict mode, the number 1 and the string "1" are still different.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: assert.throws fails when the function throws the wrong kind of error (a TypeError, not a RangeError), and also when it does not throw at all ("ok" is valid).

questions.q: Why must you write await assert.rejects(promise, /db down/), with await?
questions.explain: assert.rejects returns a promise itself. Forgetting await lets the test pass even when the promise does not reject the way you expected.
options: Because rejects only works inside a for loop
A promise settles later; without await the test can finish before the check has run
It is not needed; await is optional there

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: loadTask(99) rejects with a matching message, so the first check passes. loadTask(1) resolves, so rejects itself fails with an AssertionError.
options:
first passed
second failed: db down

questions.q: A failed deepEqual shows + done: false, and - done: true,. What do + and - mean?
questions.explain: The message starts with + actual - expected. Here the code returned done: false, but the test expected done: true.
options: + is what you expected; - is what you got
+ is what you got (actual); - is what you expected
+ lines were added to the file; - lines were deleted
+ means the test passed; - means it failed

questions.q: Why does the lesson put node --test into package.json as the test script?
questions.explain: node --test finds every test file in the project. Putting it behind npm test gives everyone the same command.
options: Because node --test only works from a script
So the whole team and CI run every test with one command, npm test
So the tests run on every npm install
So tests are published to npm

questions.q: How does a CI system know that a test failed and a pull request should be blocked?
questions.explain: An exit code of 0 means success; anything else is a failure. CI tools stop and mark the check red on a non-zero exit code.
options: It reads the word "fail" in the output
The test runner exits with code 1 when any test fails
The test runner deletes the branch
GitHub asks the author by e-mail

questions.q: TaskList calls notify, which sends an e-mail in the real app. What does a test pass in instead?
questions.explain: Tests must never send real e-mail. A mock such as mock.fn() records callCount() and each call's arguments.
options: The real e-mail function, with a test address
A mock function that records every call, so the test can check it was called with the right arguments
Nothing; tests skip functions they cannot run
A function that throws, to make sure it is never called

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: mock.calls has one entry per call, in order, and each entry's arguments is the array of arguments. calls[1] is the second call.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a fake, mock.method is a spy: the real Math.max still runs and returns 7, and the call is recorded. After restoreAll(), the real method is back and calls are no longer recorded.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call mock.restoreAll() in afterEach?
questions.explain: mock.method changes a shared object, such as mailer or Math. Restoring it after each test keeps the tests independent.
options: To make the tests run faster
To put the real methods back after every test, so one test's fake can never leak into the next
To delete the test file after it runs
Because mocks stop working after 1 second

questions.q: What should you mock in your tests?
questions.explain: A test that mocks everything only proves that the mocks work. Mock what is slow, costly or outside your control, and test your own logic for real.
options: Everything, so the tests never fail
The edges of your system: e-mail, payment providers, other services, the clock
Nothing; mocks are always a bad idea

questions.q: Test B only passes because test A added a task first. What is wrong?
questions.explain: Each test must pass on its own and in any order. Give every test a fresh start, for example with beforeEach.
options: Nothing, as long as they always run in that order
The tests are not isolated: running B alone, or changing A, breaks B for no visible reason
B should be merged into A

questions.q: The tests share one list instead of using beforeEach. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first test added a task, so the second one gets id 3. Its result depends on the other test: the classic isolation bug.

questions.q: Now every test gets a fresh list, like beforeEach. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both tests see a list with exactly one task, so both get id 2, in any order. That is test isolation.

questions.q: Which hook runs once, before all the tests in a describe?
questions.explain: before and after run once per suite; beforeEach and afterEach run around every single test.

questions.q: Why test a task store that runs SQL against a real database instead of a mock?
questions.explain: The SQL is the part most likely to be wrong. Only a real database, such as PGlite, runs it and enforces the constraints.
options: Because mocking a database is not allowed
A mock would not notice a typo in the SQL or a broken constraint
Because real databases are faster than mocks
Because it makes the test a unit test

questions.q: In the lesson's store test, why is the schema created once in before and each test given await template.clone()?
questions.explain: The second test got id 1 again for "Buy milk": its database really was a fresh copy. Fast and isolated.
options: Creating a database takes seconds; a copy of the template is much faster, and each test still gets its own clean database
So all tests share the same rows
Because PGlite can only create one database per process

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A clone is an independent copy of the template: it has the table, and its own rows. The insert into the copy never reaches the template, so the next test's clone starts empty again.

questions.q: Against a real PostgreSQL server, which database should your tests use?
questions.explain: Tests insert and delete rows. Never point them at development or production data. Recreate the tables, or wrap each test in a transaction that is rolled back.
options: The production database, so the tests see real data
Your development database, to save time
A separate test database, recreated or rolled back so each test starts clean
Whichever database is in DATABASE_URL at the moment

questions.q: The HTTP test starts its server with server.listen(0, ...). Why port 0?
questions.explain: The test then reads the real port from server.address().port. It closes the server in after.
options: Port 0 is the default HTTP port
It asks the system for any free port, so the test never clashes with another program
It makes the server reject all requests
Port 0 is only reachable from tests

questions.q: In Vitest, what replaces assert.equal(a, b), assert.deepEqual(a, b) and mock.fn()?
questions.explain: The ideas are identical; only the names differ. toBe is like === and toEqual compares content.

questions.q: What does plain npx vitest, without run, do?
questions.explain: vitest run runs once, which is what npm test and CI need. Watch mode is for while you are coding.
options: Runs the tests once and exits
Starts watch mode: it stays open and reruns the affected tests every time you save a file

questions.q: A mock can also have an implementation. What does this print?
questions.explain: mock.fn(impl) runs your implementation and still records every call. Each entry in mock.calls keeps the arguments and the result it returned.

questions.q: This is the lesson's validateTitle. What does this print?
questions.explain: The title is trimmed before it is measured, so " a " is only 1 character: a RangeError. A number is not a string: a TypeError. Tests check both the happy path and each kind of error.

questions.q: Write assertEqual(actual, expected): when they are not ===, throw an Error with the message Expected X, got Y, where X and Y are the values written with JSON.stringify.
questions.explain: At its heart, an assertion is a check that throws. JSON.stringify puts quotes around strings, which makes a stray space easy to see.

questions.q: Write assertDeepEqual(actual, expected) for plain objects and arrays: compare them by content using JSON.stringify, and throw Error("not deep-equal") when they differ. (Key order must match; that is fine here.)
questions.explain: Two separate objects are never ===, so compare their content. The real assert.deepEqual is smarter (any key order, dates, maps), but the idea is the same.

questions.q: Write assertThrows(fn, ErrorType). Call fn. If it throws an error that is an instance of ErrorType, return quietly. If it throws something else, throw Error("wrong error type"). If it does not throw at all, throw Error("missing expected exception").
questions.explain: The "missing" error must be thrown after the try/catch; thrown inside the try, your own catch would swallow it. That is the same message node:assert gives: Missing expected exception.
questions.expected:
pass
pass
fail: wrong error type
fail: missing expected exception

questions.q: Build a tiny test runner. test(name, fn) stores a test. run() calls each one: print ✔ name when it returns normally, ✖ name: message when it throws, and finally pass N fail M. One failing test must not stop the others.
questions.explain: This is what node:test does at its core: catch each test's error, keep going, and count. The real runner also exits with code 1 when anything failed.
questions.expected:
✔ adds numbers
✖ trims titles: expected " a"
✔ knows empty arrays are truthy
pass 2 fail 1

questions.q: Write mockFn(). It returns a function that records every call: fake.calls is an array with one array of arguments per call. The fake returns undefined.
questions.explain: Functions are objects, so the fake can carry its own calls array. node:test's mock.fn() works the same way, with mock.calls[i].arguments.

questions.q: Write spyOn(object, name). Replace object[name] with a wrapper that records each call's arguments in spy.calls and still calls the real method (with the right this) and returns its result. spy.restore() puts the real method back.
questions.explain: A spy watches without changing behaviour, so the real method must still run. apply(this, args) keeps this.factor working. Restoring afterwards is what mock.restoreAll() does in afterEach.

questions.q: inviteUser takes the mailer as an argument. Write a fake mailer object whose send(to, text) stores { to, text } in a sent array instead of sending anything, so the program prints what would have been sent.
questions.explain: E-mail is an edge of your system, so it is the right thing to fake. Passing the mailer in as an argument makes swapping it for a fake easy.
questions.expected:
{ invited: 'ada@example.com' }
[ { to: 'ada@example.com', text: 'Welcome to the Task API' } ]

questions.q: Finish runAll(tests, beforeEach): call beforeEach() before every test, then run the test, and return an array of "pass" or "fail" (a test fails when it throws). The tests must then pass in any order.
questions.explain: Because every test starts from the same fresh state, the order no longer matters. Calling setup only once would make the second and third tests fail.

questions.q: Write async assertRejects(promise, pattern): await the promise. If it rejects with an error whose message matches the regular expression pattern, return quietly. Otherwise throw Error("did not reject as expected").
questions.explain: A promise that resolves is a failure too. And the caller must await assertRejects(...), or the test would finish before the check runs.
questions.expected:
pass
fail: did not reject as expected
fail: did not reject as expected

questions.q: The slug function turns two spaces into two dashes. Fix slug so every run of spaces becomes one dash (and ends are trimmed). The test cases below should then all pass.
questions.explain: The tests showed exactly which inputs broke. /\s+/g matches every run of spaces, so each run becomes a single dash. Keep the test cases: they stop the bug from coming back.
